papers.title_in_file: A Review on Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm and its Variants
papers.version_note: arXiv:2306.09198v2, 26 Jun 2023; the text matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: A literature review of QAOA and its variants with a small set of the authors' own MaxCut simulations and IBM hardware runs.

existing.note: Section 3.3.1 gives the deep-circuit condition as the minimum energy gap being large enough to be resolved in the evolution time; Table 4 words it as instances with large enough spectral gaps.
Section 3.3.2 gives the same basis: the cost of the protocol comes from optimizing the variational parameters, not from the circuits.
The statement is the end of a heuristic argument in Section 3.5.2; the preceding theoretical studies are cited, not proved here.
Stated in Section 5.1 and echoed in Section 5.3. The authors scope it as a review of the literature, with their own simulations limited to MaxCut on graphs of 4 to 18 nodes.
existing.certainty_reason: Section 5.1 Summary of Analysis states the review's own conclusion.

assertions.value: The authors state that a single QAOA layer consists of a cost layer for the problem Hamiltonian and a mixer layer whose Hamiltonian does not commute with the problem Hamiltonian.
quotes: The fundamental building block, a single layer of the QAOA circuit, consists of a cost layer associated with the problem Hamiltonian and a mixer layer whose corresponding Hamiltonian does not commute with the problem Hamiltonian.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 defines the layer structure.

assertions.value: The authors state that QAOA performance is typically measured by the approximation ratio, the ratio of the cost of the solution output by QAOA to the cost of the true optimal solution.
quotes: The performance of QAOA is typically measured by the approximation ratio CQAOA/Cmax, i.e., the ratio of the cost associated with the solution output by QAOA to that of the true optimal solution.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 defines the metric.

assertions.value: The authors state that the review aims to answer whether QAOA can outperform classical algorithms and under what circumstances it should be used, and that the literature holds conflicting opinions on these points.
quotes: literature still contains many conflicting opinions on various aspects of the algorithm, such as for which problems, if any, QAOA can outperform classical algorithms and whether it can provide any practical quantum advantage under the noise and errors of current quantum devices.
whether QAOA can outperform classical algorithms and under what circumstances it should be used.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 states the review's aim.
assertions.reader_inference: Scope statement; the review is a literature review plus a small set of its own simulations.

assertions.value: The authors state that their own experiments use custom implementations of six QAOA variants on MaxCut graphs of 4 to 18 nodes, that 78 graphs were generated, and that the results are part of an ongoing study.
quotes: A total of 78 graphs where generated for the results we report here.
with sizes ranging from 4 to 18 nodes.
The results presented here are part of an ongoing study
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.2 and the Table 5 caption give the experimental scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that they used the COBYLA optimizer with a tolerance of 0.0002 or at most 500 iterations, layer depths from 1 to 8, and random initial parameters except for WS-QAOA.
quotes: The optimizer iterated until convergence based on the specified tolerance level (0.0002) or until 500 iterations, whichever came first.
ranging from 1 to 8 layers.
Except for "WS-QAOA", which provides a specific initialization of the parameters, we randomly initialized the parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.2 gives the settings.

assertions.value: The authors state that their hardware runs used IBM Quantum Falcon r5.11H processors named ibm_oslo, ibm_lagos, ibm_nairobi and ibm_perth.
quotes: specifically the IBM Quantum Falcon r5.11H quantum processors, which include the ibm_oslo, ibm_lagos, ibm_nairobi and ibm_perth.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.2 names the devices.

assertions.value: The authors state that the iteration cap only affected ma-QAOA, which often reached the cap and needed many thousands of iterations for a slightly higher approximation ratio, and that unconstrained runs are planned.
quotes: The maximum number of iterations only influenced ma-QAOA, which often reached the maximum cap of iterations and needed many thousands of iterations to achieve just a slightly higher approximation ratio.
However, we will include the unconstrained versions in the future release of our results.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.2 states the limit on its own experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that their curated results leave out numerous findings, that newer variants such as ADAPT-QAOA and RecursiveQAOA are not yet included, and that more graph types, sizes and optimizers are planned.
quotes: numerous findings and results could not be included in this review paper.
including newer variants such as the ADAPT-QAOA and RecursiveQAOA.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.4 states the limits of the experiments.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in simulations, all variants reached mean approximation ratios as high as 0.98 on complete graphs and as high as 0.94 on regular graphs, and at most 0.92 on random graphs.
quotes: all variants demonstrate superior approximation ratios when applied to complete and regular graphs, achieving mean ratios as high as 0.98, for complete graphs, and as high as 0.94 for regular graphs on simulations.
when applied to random graphs, the approximation ratio drops to at most 0.92.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study run by the review's authors.

assertions.value: The authors report that for QAOA in noise-free simulation the mean approximation ratio fell from 0.98 (regular) and 0.94 (random) at 4 nodes to 0.83 and 0.76 at 18 nodes, and that for random graphs of 18 nodes the ratio typically lies between 0.6 and 0.8.
quotes: for QAOA, the approximation ratio falls from 0.98 and 0.94 (regular and random, respectively) for 4 nodes to 0.83 and 0.76 for 18 nodes.
in random graphs of 18 nodes the approximation ratio typically lies between 0.6 and 0.8.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study run by the review's authors.
assertions.reader_inference: At 18 nodes the ratios are well below the 0.878 Goemans-Williamson guarantee the review cites for the worst case, but the paper runs no classical baseline of its own, so no comparison is made in this study.

assertions.value: The authors report in their summary table of simulation results a mean approximation ratio of 0.88 for ma-QAOA with 450.97 circuit calls, against 0.87 and 108.25 for QAOA, 0.87 and 104.31 for FALQON, 0.84 and 287.16 for QAOA+, 0.79 and 99.28 for WS-QAOA, and 0.72 and 95.72 for ModifiedQAOA.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study run by the review's authors.
assertions.reader_inference: ma-QAOA's cap of 500 iterations (Section 4.2) bounds the circuit-call count in this table.

assertions.value: The authors report that circuit layer depth had a varying effect on the approximation ratio and seemed less significant than the other factors studied, for depths up to p = 8.
quotes: it seems to not be as significant as the other factors discussed, at least for depths up to p = 8.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study run by the review's authors.

assertions.value: The authors report that real IBM hardware gave a significant reduction in mean approximation ratios for all six variants compared with noise-free simulation; in their comparison table, QAOA fell from 0.899 to 0.702 and ma-QAOA from 0.936 to 0.732.
quotes: The real quantum hardware results show a significant reduction in the mean approximation ratios across all the variants
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study run by the review's authors.
assertions.reader_inference: On hardware the six variants end within 0.702 to 0.732, a much smaller spread than in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that mean cosine similarity between initial and optimized parameters was above 0.96 for QAOA, QAOA+, ModifiedQAOA, WS-QAOA and ma-QAOA and about 0.51 for FALQON, and they read the high values as COBYLA possibly not exploring the parameter space thoroughly.
quotes: high mean cosine similarity values (greater than 0.96) suggest that the optimization process may not be thoroughly exploring the parameter space.
FALQON's significantly lower mean cosine similarity (approximately 0.51)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study run by the review's authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors' reading is a hypothesis; the study does not test it with another optimizer.

assertions.value: The review reports that, citing Crooks, QAOA for MaxCut on an n-node graph is expected to need gates of order n squared times p and a run time of order n times p, against run time of order n times m for Goemans-Williamson, and that this suggests a speedup for dense graphs.
quotes: QAOA for MaxCut on an n-node graph is expected to require O(n2p) gates and have a run time of O(np)
the classical Goemans-Williamson (GW) algorithm requires a run time of O(nm)
QAOA, even at modest depths, may offer a speedup over its classical counterpart for dense graphs.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.
assertions.reader_inference: The review notes the O(np) run time assumes O(n) gates run in parallel.

assertions.value: The review reports that Zhang et al. ran QAOA with 2 to 10 layers on a minimum vertex cover instance of 10 vertices and 16 edges and concluded that QAOA gives an exponential acceleration for large MVC problems.
quotes: (2 ≤ p ≤ 10) to find the MVC on an undirected graph consisting of 10 vertices and 16 edges.
the authors concluded that QAOA provides an exponential acceleration for large MVC problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.
assertions.reader_inference: The cited conclusion extends a complexity comparison from one 10-vertex instance to large problems; the review reports it without comment.

assertions.value: The review reports that Ebadi et al. found, on deep-circuit instances, that the probability of observing a maximum independent set scales with exponent 1.03 for simulated annealing and 0.63 for QAOA in the difficulty parameter eta.
quotes: for SA, the probability of observing an MIS scales as PMIS = 1 − exp −Cη−1.03
QAOA gave rise to an improved scaling, PMIS = 1 − exp −Cη−0.63
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.
assertions.reader_inference: Supports the stored Ebadi assertion; the exponents are the quantitative basis of the superlinear claim.

assertions.value: The review reports that Guerreschi and Matsuura concluded QAOA must run in at most a minute to compete with classical solvers on problems with fewer than 400 variables, and that a speedup for a specific combinatorial problem needs several hundred qubits.
quotes: QAOA must run in a maximum of a minute to compete with classical solvers
on problems with less than 400 variables. It would only be possible to achieve a quantum speedup for a specific combinatorial problem once several hundreds of qubits are available.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Guerreschi and Matsuura suggested the exponential cost of the QAOA protocol comes not from the complexity of the quantum circuits but from the challenge of optimizing the variational parameters.
quotes: They suggested that the reason for the exponential cost of the QAOA protocol is not due to the complexity of the quantum circuits but rather the challenge of optimizing the variational parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the basis of the stored near-term-speedup assertion.

assertions.value: The review reports that Shaydulin et al., with a budget of 1000 optimization steps and 1000 measurements per cost value, estimated about 16 minutes for a complete QAOA optimization, orders of magnitude above state-of-the-art classical AKMAXSAT solvers.
quotes: With a budget of 1000 optimization steps and an optimistic assumption of 1000 measurements needed for obtaining the statistics to calculate the cost function value
the estimated time cost for a complete QAOA optimization is about 16 minutes, which is orders of magnitude greater than the runtime of classical state-of-the-art AKMAXSAT solvers [151].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Sanders et al. concluded that a quantum optimization algorithm with only a quadratic speedup is unlikely to give quantum advantage on early fault-tolerant surface-code processors without improvements such as faster state distillation.
quotes: they concluded that any quantum optimization algorithm offering only a quadratic speedup is unlikely to produce any quantum advantage on these processors unless significant improvements in the surface code implementation, such as faster state distillation, are in place.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Larkin et al. reduced the training-phase execution time for MaxCut on random 3-regular graphs by two orders of magnitude compared with earlier estimates, and found QAOA runtime competitive with an exact, an approximate and a heuristic classical solver, with further study needed on other graph types and larger sizes.
quotes: reduce the execution time for MaxCut on random 3-regular graphs by two orders of magnitude
the runtime performance of the QAOA was competitive concerning the aforementioned solvers.
further studies are required to assess the effectiveness and scalability of this approach
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Lykov et al. found that the main obstacle to a QAOA advantage over classical solvers is the exponential sampling time for large graphs, and suggested a QAOA circuit needs depth p above 11 to match classical algorithms on large graphs.
quotes: According to their results, the main obstacle to QAOA's advantage over classical solvers is the exponential sampling time required for large graph sizes.
a QAOA circuit must be implemented with depth p > 11 to match the performance of classical algorithms for large graph sizes
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that the Goemans-Williamson algorithm guarantees an approximation ratio of at least 0.87856 for MaxCut, and that under the Unique Games Conjecture this is the best possible for any polynomial-time algorithm.
quotes: the algorithm guarantees an approximation ratio of at least 0.87856, ensuring that the obtained cut weights at least 87.856% of the optimal cut's weight [40, 53].
Under the Unique Games Conjecture, this approximation ratio is the best possible for any polynomial-time algorithm [54].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review states that Håstad conjectured that achieving an approximation ratio above 16/17, about 0.9412, is NP-hard for MaxCut.
quotes: Håstad [39] conjectured that achieving an approximation ratio higher than 16/17 ≃ 0.9412 is NP-hard
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.
assertions.reader_inference: The review uses the word conjectured; Håstad's paper is cited as [39] and not read here.

assertions.value: The review reports that Farhi et al. proved QAOA at one layer with optimal angles gives a cut of at least 0.6924 times the optimal on any 3-regular graph, against 0.5 for random guessing, and that extending the analysis to higher p is hard because of the double-exponential growth of the classical parameter-finding cost.
quotes: QAOA1 on any 3-regular graph will always produce a cut whose size is at least 0.6924 times the size of the optimal cut
which yields α = 0.5.
due to the double-exponential growth of the complexity of the classical algorithm used to find optimal parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Farhi et al. conjectured, and Mbeng et al. later proved, that on rings of size above 2p QAOA at p layers achieves α ≥ (2p+1)/(2p+2), so solutions can approach the optimum arbitrarily closely at large p.
quotes: On 2-regular graphs, also known as the ring of disagrees, they conjectured that on rings of size n > 2p, QAOAp can achieve α ≥ (2p+1)/(2p+2), which was later proved by Mbeng et al. [159].
at large p, QAOA can produce solutions arbitrarily close to the true optima on the ring of disagrees.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Wurtz and Love found α ≥ 0.7559 at p = 2 on 3-regular graphs of girth above 5 and α ≥ 0.7924 at p = 3 on graphs of girth above 7, and that up to p = 3 QAOA does not outperform the best classical algorithms in the worst case on 3-regular graphs.
quotes: for p = 2, α ≥ 0.7559 on 3-regular graphs with girth > 5.
For p = 3, α ≥ 0.7924 on graphs with girth > 7.
it also showed that up to p = 3, QAOA is not able to outperform the best classical algorithms on 3-regular graphs in the worst-case scenario
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Hastings showed a one-step classical threshold algorithm beats QAOA at one layer on triangle-free MaxCut, with c about 0.335, and that numerics for 2 ≤ D < 1000 showed it winning on all triangle-free instances.
quotes: Numerical calculations revealed that for all 2 ≤ D < 1000, a single step of this classical algorithm would outperform QAOA1 on all triangle-free MaxCut instances.
with c ≈ 0.335.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Marwaha showed by direct calculation, for degrees 2 ≤ D < 500 and girth above 5, a 2-local classical MaxCut algorithm that outperforms QAOA at two layers, with c stabilizing near 0.417 against 0.407 for QAOA at two layers.
quotes: for degrees 2 ≤ D < 500 and every D-regular graph G of girth > 5, while QAOA2 has a larger expected cut fraction than QAOA1 on G
stabilizes at around 0.417 in the asymptotic limit, compared with that of QAOA2, c ≈ 0.407.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Farhi et al. computed QAOA on the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model at infinite size for 1 ≤ p ≤ 12 and found V11 ≥ 0.6393 above 2/π, the classical SDP value, and V12 ≥ 0.6466, with values for 9 ≤ p ≤ 12 not optimized but extrapolated.
quotes: they numerically computed the QAOA performance for 1 ≤ p ≤ 12
at p = 11, QAOA already outperforms the classical SDP algorithm mentioned above, where V ̄11 ≥ 0.6393 > 2/π.
At p = 12, QAOA produces V ̄12 ≥ 0.6466.
for 9 ≤ p ≤ 12, the values of Vp(γ, β) were not optimized but evaluated at some parameters extrapolated from those at lower p
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Basso et al. evaluated QAOA on large-girth D-regular graphs up to p = 20 in the large-D limit and found that from p = 11 QAOA beats the classical local algorithm of Barak and Marwaha, and that they conjectured QAOA reaches the Parisi value as p goes to infinity, which is not rigorously proven.
quotes: the authors could perform numerical evaluations up to p = 20 in the large D limit.
the classical local algorithm for MaxCut on large-girth random regular graphs considered by Barak and Marwaha [162].
However, this remains to be rigorously proven.
QAOA at p ≥ 11 could outperform the assumption-free classical SDP algorithms in solving the MaxCut problem on D-regular graphs
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Barak and Marwaha proved that for every p a polynomial-time classical p-local algorithm exists for D-regular graphs of girth above 2p + 1, whose guarantee tends to 1/2 + (2/π)/√D at large degree and girth, surpassing QAOA at one and two layers but not reaching the optimal Parisi value.
quotes: It was proved that for every p, there exists a polynomial-time classical p-local algorithm for all D-regular graphs of girth > 2p + 1
Nevertheless, neither of these two classical algorithms achieves the optimal Parisi value.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Hastings showed a simple modification of the classical algorithm, the Gaussian wave process, can achieve some c above 2/π, though c was not optimized, and that it is therefore unclear whether QAOA can outperform any classical algorithm for MaxCut on D-regular graphs.
quotes: the Gaussian wave process, can also achieve some other c > 2/π
it is still unclear if QAOA can outperform any classical algorithm for MaxCut on D-regular graphs.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Marwaha and Hadfield found that QAOA at one layer starts outperforming the classical threshold algorithm on triangle-free Max-kXOR in the large-degree limit when k > 4, and that this does not rule out a different local tensor algorithm matching or beating QAOA at larger k.
quotes: they found that when k > 4, QAOA1 starts outperforming the threshold algorithm in the large degree limit, demonstrating a quantum advantage.
this does not rule out the possibility that a different local tensor algorithm [95] will match or outperform QAOA at larger
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Boulebnane and Montanaro found, analytically and numerically for random 8-SAT, that QAOA at depth p of about 14 would match the classical WalkSATlm algorithm, with the extent of any advantage unclear because small-instance medians deviate as p grows.
quotes: QAOA with a depth p ≈ 14 would match the performance of a random-local-search-based classical algorithm
the extent of the advantage is still unclear
the performance of QAOA on random 8-SAT instances.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Bravyi et al. proved a limitation of fixed-depth QAOA on bipartite D-regular graphs: the bound approaches about 0.833 at large D, below the Goemans-Williamson bound 0.8786, so QAOA there cannot outperform the best classical algorithm.
quotes: first realized a limitation of fixed-depth QAOA in solving the MaxCut problem on bipartite D-regular
≈ 0.833, which falls behind the GW bound 0.8786, indicating that QAOA, in this case, cannot outperform the best classical algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Farhi et al. proved that in the low-depth regime p ≲ ε log n QAOA fails to produce an independent set larger than 0.854 times the optimal as D goes to infinity, using the overlap gap property.
quotes: They proved that in the low-depth regime p ≲ ε log n, QAOA fails to produce an independent set larger than 0.854 times the optimal as D → ∞.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Basso et al. established that any constant-p QAOA is bounded away from optimality on dense k-spin models for every even k ≥ 4 because of the overlap gap property, and notes that a quantum advantage remains possible beyond sub-logarithmic depth because classical AMP is also suboptimal there.
quotes: is still bounded away from optimality on dense k-spin models for any even k ≥ 4 due to the obstruction by the OGP.
potential quantum advantage is still possible in these problems, particularly when QAOA surpasses sub-logarithmic depths
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Bae and Lee showed analytically that level-1 RQAOA reaches approximation ratio 1 for MaxCut on complete graphs with 2n vertices, while original QAOA at p = 1 is strictly bounded below 1.
quotes: MaxCut problem on complete graphs with 2n vertices.
the level-1 RQAOA achieves the approximation ratio 1
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Crooks simulated QAOA on 10-node Erdős-Rényi graphs with 50% edge probability for up to p = 32 and found that QAOA started to outperform Goemans-Williamson at p = 6, and consistently so for p ≥ 8 for sizes 6 to 17 nodes.
quotes: By considering 10-node random graphs generated from the Erdős-Rényi configuration with a 50% edge probability, the author measured the average approximation ratio of QAOA for up to p = 32
at p = 6, QAOA starts to outperform the classical GW algorithm.
for p ≥ 8, the quantum algorithm consistently outperforms the GW algorithm across different problem sizes
ranging from n = 6 to n = 17
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Lotshaw et al. studied all connected non-isomorphic graphs with n ≤ 9 vertices up to p = 3 and found QAOA exceeds the worst-case Goemans-Williamson bound on most of them by p = 3.
quotes: all connected non-isomorphic graphs with n ≤ 9 vertices.
on most graphs with n ≤ 9, QAOA exceeds the worst-case GW bound even by p = 3
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Moussa et al. found QAOA outperformed Goemans-Williamson on most 4-regular graphs up to 24 nodes at p = 10, and that an ML model predicted instances where QAOA wins with up to 96% cross-validated accuracy.
quotes: QAOA outperformed GW on most instances of 4-regular graphs up to 24 nodes at depth p = 10.
The proposed ML model achieved up to 96% cross-validated accuracy in predictions.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.
assertions.reader_inference: The review itself cautions that the finding holds for the specific parameters and scenarios studied.

assertions.value: The review reports that Sreedhar et al. simulated QAOA with matrix product states of limited bond dimension up to p = 100 and concluded entanglement plays a minor role in solving the MaxCut and Exact Cover 3 problems studied, with the interplay on other problems left open.
quotes: entanglement plays a minor role in solving the MaxCut and Exact Cover 3 problems studied
high depths, up to p = 100.
the interplay between entanglement and circuit depth and their impact on the QAOA performance in other problem instances remains an open research problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Herrman et al., studying connected non-isomorphic graphs with at most eight vertices up to p = 3, found graphs without odd cycles have a 12% higher mean probability of obtaining an optimal solution than graphs with odd cycles.
quotes: graphs without odd cycles have a 12% higher mean probability of obtaining an optimal solution than those with odd cycles.
performance of QAOA with up to p = 3 for the MaxCut problem
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Willsch et al. found QAOA with p = 1 to 5 could not compete with quantum annealing on the instances tried when no minor embedding was needed, and that the D-Wave machine even beat QAOA run on a simulator.
quotes: The study also found that for the set of problem instances considered, QAOA with p = 1, . . . , 5 could not compete with quantum annealing when no minor embedding was necessary: the D-Wave machine was even able to outperform QAOA executed on a simulator.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Harrigan et al. ran QAOA up to p = 5 on a 23-qubit superconducting processor and found performance on hardware-grid problems independent of problem size, rising up to p = 3 and degrading at p = 4 and p = 5, while for MaxCut on 3-regular graphs and the SK model performance fell with problem size yet stayed above random guessing.
quotes: up to p = 5 on a superconducting quantum processor with 23 physical qubits.
the performance increased with circuit depth up to p = 3; however, the noise degraded the performance for p = 4 and p = 5.
QAOA's performance decreased with problem size but still provided an advantage over random guessing.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Pagano et al. ran QAOA on a trapped-ion computer with 20 to 40 qubits and found performance did not degrade significantly with size, while going from p = 1 to p = 2 did not significantly improve performance because of decoherence and bit-flip errors.
quotes: The study also indicated that increasing the number of QAOA layers from p = 1 to p = 2 did not significantly improve the performance of QAOA due to the limitations imposed by the hardware, such as decoherence and bit-flip errors.
ranging from 20 to 40.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review's table of hardware experiments reports that on a trapped-ion Quantinuum device solution quality increased monotonically with p up to 10 for all problem instances, with largest α = 0.94, and its discussion states this was for graphs of 20 qubits.
quotes: Solution quality increased monotonically with p up to 10 for all problem instances, with largest α = 0.94.
a monotonic improvement in the performance of QAOA with up to 10 layers for graphs consisting of 20 qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Niroula et al. ran XY-QAOA circuits on up to 20 qubits of a trapped-ion computer for extractive summarization and state that quantum advantage is near for variational quantum algorithms.
quotes: They effectively implemented XY-QAOA circuits on up to 20 qubits
quantum advantage is near for variational quantum algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.
assertions.reader_inference: This cited optimism sits against the review's own Section 5.1 conclusion that a general advantage is an open question and unlikely on near-term devices.

assertions.value: The review reports that theoretical studies showed QAOA performance, measured by output fidelity and approximation ratio, degrades as a power law in the noise strength, with the power proportional to the system size, so an optimal number of layers exists for a given noise rate.
quotes: Theoretical studies showed that the QAOA performance, characterized by the output state fidelity and the approximation ratio, degrades as a power law with the noise strength, with the power being proportional to the system size [212, 213].
an optimal number of layers can be determined for QAOA for any given noise rate.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the review attributes to other work; not tested in the review.

assertions.value: The review reports that Lotshaw et al. showed, under a local noise model, that the number of measurements needed to reproduce the noiseless distribution increases exponentially with the gate error rates, which limits near-term scalability.
quotes: Lotshaw et al. [214] showed that the number of measurements needed to achieve the above goal increases exponentially with the gate error rates
